content.study:
Joint tortfeasors are two or more persons whose conduct makes them jointly responsible for the same tortious injury; in composite negligence, the claimant has not contributed to the accident and may ordinarily recover the whole proved loss from any liable joint tortfeasor, subject to the law governing contribution between the wrongdoers.

Joint liability must be distinguished from contributory negligence. The claimant's own negligence is relevant to contributory negligence; where the claimant is innocent and two or more defendants jointly cause the same damage, the defendants may be jointly and severally liable to the claimant.

This topic is included as a dedicated Torts coverage unit so students can distinguish the doctrine from neighbouring causes of action and apply it to factual problems.

sections.heading: Doctrinal Foundations
sections.body: Joint liability must be distinguished from contributory negligence. The claimant's own negligence is relevant to contributory negligence; where the claimant is innocent and two or more defendants jointly cause the same damage, the defendants may be jointly and severally liable to the claimant.

sections.heading: Essential Elements
sections.body: 1. Two or more persons contribute to the same actionable injury or are jointly responsible for the same tort. 2. The claimant has suffered one indivisible loss attributable to the defendants' conduct. 3. For composite negligence, the claimant did not contribute to the accident. 4. The claimant proves the actionable duty, breach, causation and recoverable damage. 5. Any inter se contribution or apportionment is treated separately from the claimant's right to recover the proved loss.

learningObjectives: Define joint tortfeasors and composite negligence in the Indian law of torts, identifying how multiple wrongdoers cause indivisible injury.

Differentiate composite negligence (where an innocent claimant recovers full damages jointly and severally from any wrongdoer) from contributory negligence (where claimant's own negligence reduces recovery).

Master the four core propositions of Khenyei v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. ((2015) 9 SCC 273) governing impleadment, non-apportionment vis-a-vis claimants, and inter se contribution between tortfeasors.
Explain the procedure for inter se execution and independent contribution claims under CPC Order I and the Motor Vehicles Act claims framework.
enhancement.definition: Joint tortfeasors are two or more persons whose concurrent or concerted wrongful acts cause a single, indivisible tortious injury to the plaintiff. In composite negligence, where two or more wrongdoers negligently cause an accident without any fault on the part of the injured claimant, each wrongdoer is jointly and severally liable to the claimant for the entire compensation.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: As settled by the 3-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court in Khenyei v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. ((2015) 9 SCC 273), the liability of joint tortfeasors in cases of composite negligence is joint and several. The claimant is entitled to sue all or any of the joint tortfeasors and recover the whole amount of damages from any one of them; apportionment of liability between tortfeasors cannot be forced upon the claimant. Inter se apportionment is permissible solely to determine contribution between the wrongdoers, which may be recovered in execution if both are parties, or by separate suit if one was not impleaded. Unlike contributory negligence, an innocent victim's claim cannot be reduced or bifurcated.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Indian common law of torts received under Article 372; Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Order I Rule 1 & Rule 3 for joinder of parties, Order I Rule 10, Section 9 for maintainability of civil suits, Section 47 & Order XXI for execution); Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) principles and Law Reform (Married Women and Tortfeasors) Act principles received as justice, equity, and good conscience; Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (Sections 165-175 for Claims Tribunal procedure); Limitation Act, 1963 (Article 113 for contribution actions); Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 for proof of negligence.
essentialIngredients: 1. Multiplicity of Wrongdoers: Two or more persons commit wrongful acts or omissions resulting in the same injury, whether acting in concert (joint tortfeasors strictly so called) or independently producing a single indivisible damage (composite negligence).
2. Single Indivisible Damage: The wrongful conduct of each defendant results in one common injury or indivisible harm to the claimant.
3. Absence of Claimant Fault: For composite negligence to apply, the injured claimant must be innocent of any contributory negligence that caused or contributed to the accident.
4. Joint and Several Liability: The claimant has the unfettered option to sue all, some, or any one of the joint tortfeasors and recover the entire compensation from the chosen solvent defendant.

5. Distinct Inter Se Contribution: Determination of relative blame (apportionment) is strictly an internal equity between the tortfeasors and does not impair or delay the claimant's right to full recovery.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Joint tortfeasors are two or more persons whose conduct makes them jointly responsible for the same tortious injury; in composite negligence, the claimant has not contributed to the accident and may ordinarily recover the whole proved loss from any liable joint tortfeasor, subject to the law governing contribution between the wrongdoers.

Joint liability must be distinguished from contributory negligence. The claimant's own negligence is relevant to contributory negligence; where the claimant is innocent and two or more defendants jointly cause the same damage, the defendants may be jointly and severally liable to the claimant.

In Khenyei v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. ((2015) 9 SCC 273), a 3-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court resolved longstanding conflicts among High Court Full Benches and definitively laid down the four controlling propositions of composite negligence in India:

1. Entitlement to Sue Any or All: The claimant is entitled to sue both or any one of the joint tortfeasors and recover the entire compensation; the liability is joint and several.

2. No Apportionment Against Claimant: Vis-a-vis the claimant, apportionment of compensation between the tortfeasors is not permissible. The claimant can recover the whole damages from any of them at their option.

3. Inter Se Apportionment for Contribution: If all joint tortfeasors are impleaded and evidence is sufficient, the tribunal or court may determine their inter se negligence. However, this is solely to enable the tortfeasor who pays the whole sum to recover the apportioned share from the co-tortfeasor in execution proceedings, without requiring an independent civil suit.

4. Non-Impleaded Joint Tortfeasor: The court should not attempt to determine the negligence of a non-impleaded joint tortfeasor in their absence. The paying tortfeasor retains the right to initiate independent proceedings for contribution against the non-impleaded party.
examples: Illustration 1 — Head-On Collision & Innocent Passenger: A passenger travelling in a public bus is seriously injured when the bus collides with a rashly driven trailer-truck. The passenger was entirely blameless. Under Khenyei ((2015) 9 SCC 273), this is a classic case of composite negligence: the passenger may sue either the bus owner/insurer, or the truck owner/insurer, or both, and recover 100% of the compensation from the bus insurer without any deduction for the truck's share of fault.

Illustration 2 — Execution Recovery between Joint Tortfeasors: Both the bus insurer and truck owner are impleaded before the tribunal, and evidence establishes that the truck driver was 2/3rd negligent and the bus driver 1/3rd negligent. The claimant recovers the entire award from the bus insurer. The bus insurer is entitled to recover the 2/3rd share directly from the truck owner in execution proceedings arising out of the same award without filing a separate suit.
enhancement.problemApplication:
Problem: An innocent motorcyclist's pillion rider is severely injured in a collision between the motorcycle and a negligently driven private car. The pillion rider files a claim petition against only the owner and insurer of the car. The car insurer contends that the motorcycle driver was 60% at fault, that the claim is defective for non-joinder of the motorcycle owner/driver, and that the car insurer is liable for only 40% of the damages.

Application & Assessment: (1) Under Khenyei v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. ((2015) 9 SCC 273), this is a case of composite negligence because the pillion rider did not contribute to the accident. (2) The liability of the two drivers is joint and several. The claimant has absolute discretion to sue either or both wrongdoers; the claim cannot be dismissed for non-joinder of the motorcycle driver. (3) Apportionment of compensation vis-a-vis the claimant is impermissible; the car insurer must satisfy 100% of the award. (4) Because the motorcycle driver was not impleaded, the tribunal cannot determine their negligence in their absence; the car insurer must satisfy the award and may subsequently sue the motorcycle owner/driver in independent proceedings for contribution.
keyTakeaways: Composite negligence occurs when two or more wrongdoers cause indivisible injury to an innocent claimant; liability is joint and several.
Under Khenyei ((2015) 9 SCC 273), the claimant may recover the whole compensation from any one joint tortfeasor; no apportionment can be imposed on the claimant.
Inter se apportionment of fault between joint tortfeasors is solely for contribution; if both are impleaded, the paying tortfeasor recovers the excess in execution without a fresh suit.
Contributory negligence differs fundamentally: it involves claimant fault resulting in proportional deduction of damages.

Confirmed (para 18): In composite negligence, claimant is entitled to sue both or any one of the joint tortfeasors and recover entire compensation; liability of joint tortfeasors is joint and several.
Confirmed (para 18): Apportionment of compensation between tortfeasors vis-a-vis the claimant is not permissible; claimant can recover whole damages from any solvent defendant.

Confirmed (para 18): Where all joint tortfeasors are impleaded, court/tribunal may determine inter se negligence for contribution, and paying tortfeasor can recover from co-tortfeasor in execution proceedings without an independent suit.
Confirmed (para 18): Court should not determine composite negligence of non-impleaded drivers in their absence; paying tortfeasor may sue in independent proceedings for contribution.

Confirmed (paras 14-16): Fundamental distinction between composite negligence (multiple wrongdoers, innocent victim, joint & several liability) and contributory negligence (victim's own negligence, proportionate deduction).

distinctions.title: Composite Negligence versus Contributory Negligence
distinctions.left: Composite Negligence: Wrongful acts of two or more independent wrongdoers causing single indivisible harm to an innocent victim; liability is joint and several; victim recovers 100% of loss from any liable defendant (Khenyei).
distinctions.right: Contributory Negligence: Failure of the injured victim to exercise reasonable care for their own safety, contributing to the harm; damages are proportionately reduced based on the victim's degree of fault.

rows.left: Claimant is blameless and did not contribute to the accident
rows.right: Claimant's own negligent act/omission contributed to the accident

rows.left: No deduction; claimant recovers full compensation from any defendant
rows.right: Damages are proportionately reduced to the extent of claimant's fault

rows.left: Joint and several liability among co-defendants
rows.right: Severable reduction of claimant's actionable loss

distinctions.title: Joint Tortfeasors in Concert versus Independent Concurrent Tortfeasors
distinctions.left: Joint Tortfeasors in Concert: Persons who act in furtherance of a common design or joint enterprise (or principal-agent / employer-employee relationship) committing the same tort.
distinctions.right: Independent Concurrent Tortfeasors: Persons acting entirely independently without agreement whose acts concur to produce a single indivisible injury (e.g. drivers of two colliding vehicles in composite negligence).

rows.left: Present; concerted action or common unlawful purpose
rows.right: Absent; independent negligent acts producing indivisible harm

rows.left: Joint and several liability for the entire resulting injury
rows.right: Joint and several liability under the rule in Khenyei

caseLaw.name: Khenyei v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
caseLaw.holding: Judgment dated 07/05/2015 by a 3-Judge Bench (H.L. Dattu C.J.I., S.A. Bobde, and Arun Mishra JJ.). The Supreme Court settled the law on composite negligence and joint tortfeasors: (i) In composite negligence, the claimant is entitled to sue all or any one of the joint tortfeasors and recover the entire compensation jointly and severally; (ii) Apportionment of compensation between tortfeasors vis-a-vis the claimant is not permissible, and the claimant can recover whole damages from any of them; (iii) Determination of inter se negligence between joint tortfeasors is solely for contribution between them, and where all tortfeasors are impleaded, the paying tortfeasor can recover the excess share from the co-tortfeasor in execution proceedings without an independent suit; (iv) A non-impleaded tortfeasor's negligence should not be determined in their absence, leaving the paying tortfeasor to sue independently for contribution.
caseLaw.relevance: Landmark 3-Judge Bench Supreme Court authority governing joint tortfeasors and composite negligence in India, affirming joint and several liability and prohibiting forced apportionment against innocent claimants.
